      "observed": "The LTC4412 ideal-diode controller U6 has its VIN pin (U6.1) on the USB-C input net USBC_VBUS_IN and its SENSE pin (U6.6) on the board +5V rail, but the external P-channel MOSFET Q1 is wired with its Source (Q1.2) on +5V (the SENSE/output side) and its Drain (Q1.3) on USBC_VBUS_IN (the VIN/input side).",
      "expected": "For an LTC4412 power-path / reverse-current-protection stage the P-MOSFET Source must connect to the input being OR-ed (USBC_VBUS_IN, the VIN node) and the Drain to the protected output (+5V, the SENSE node). This is also the convention the designer uses elsewhere (Q6 and Q9, both AO3401A high-side switches, have Source on the input +5V). With the Source on +5V the Q1 body diode conducts from the board +5V rail back into the USB-C port, and the controller cannot pull the gate to the Source potential to turn the FET off under reverse conditions, so the stated reverse-current protection is defeated.",
      "evidence": [
        {"source": "netlist", "quote": "(node (ref \"Q1\") (pin \"2\") (pinfunction \"S\") (pintype \"passive\"))"},

        {"source": "spec", "quote": "USB input \"OR-ing\"/protection circuitry (LTC4412 ideal-diode controller, U6)"},
        {"source": "spec", "quote": "need reverse current protection mostly"}
      ],
      "impact": "The USB-C ideal-diode OR-ing path is inverted: the board's +5V rail can back-feed into a connected USB host/device through Q1's body diode and the controller cannot properly turn the FET off under reverse conditions, so the reverse-current protection the design was built to provide does not work (and the USB port may be back-powered).",
      "confidence": 0.55
    }
  ],
  "summary": "Most of the design matches the spec (16 MHz CAN crystals, SM712 TVS arrays, MCP2515+isolated-transceiver CAN buses, e-stop buffer chain, GLOBAL_EN direct to SW1, fixed-5V LM2576, correct TPS61040 divider). The one deviation supported by the files is that the LTC4412's external P-MOSFET Q1 is installed source-to-+5V / drain-to-USB-VBUS, i.e. reversed relative to the datasheet ideal-diode connection and to the designer's own Q6/Q9 convention, which defeats the stated USB reverse-current protection."

anomalies.observed: The LTC4412 ideal-diode controller U6 has its VIN pin (U6.1) on the USB-C input net USBC_VBUS_IN and its SENSE pin (U6.6) on the board +5V rail, but the external P-channel MOSFET Q1 is wired with its Source (Q1.2) on +5V (the SENSE/output side) and its Drain (Q1.3) on USBC_VBUS_IN (the VIN/input side).
anomalies.expected: For an LTC4412 power-path / reverse-current-protection stage the P-MOSFET Source must connect to the input being OR-ed (USBC_VBUS_IN, the VIN node) and the Drain to the protected output (+5V, the SENSE node). This is also the convention the designer uses elsewhere (Q6 and Q9, both AO3401A high-side switches, have Source on the input +5V). With the Source on +5V the Q1 body diode conducts from the board +5V rail back into the USB-C port, and the controller cannot pull the gate to the Source potential to turn the FET off under reverse conditions, so the stated reverse-current protection is defeated.

evidence.quote: USB input "OR-ing"/protection circuitry (LTC4412 ideal-diode controller, U6)

anomalies.impact: The USB-C ideal-diode OR-ing path is inverted: the board's +5V rail can back-feed into a connected USB host/device through Q1's body diode and the controller cannot properly turn the FET off under reverse conditions, so the reverse-current protection the design was built to provide does not work (and the USB port may be back-powered).

parsed.summary: Most of the design matches the spec (16 MHz CAN crystals, SM712 TVS arrays, MCP2515+isolated-transceiver CAN buses, e-stop buffer chain, GLOBAL_EN direct to SW1, fixed-5V LM2576, correct TPS61040 divider). The one deviation supported by the files is that the LTC4412's external P-MOSFET Q1 is installed source-to-+5V / drain-to-USB-VBUS, i.e. reversed relative to the datasheet ideal-diode connection and to the designer's own Q6/Q9 convention, which defeats the stated USB reverse-current protection.

response.reasoning:
Let me carefully review this PCB design against the specification.

First, let me understand the intended design from the spec:
- CM4 motherboard for a precision farming rover
- Motor control via CAN buses (spec notes README says RS-485 but actual hardware is CAN)
- Two isolated CAN buses (CAN0, CAN1), each driven by MCP2515 SPI CAN controllers (U8, U9) through isolated CAN transceiver (U11/companion), broken out on M12 connectors J2 (CAN Interface A) and J13 (CAN Interface B)
- E-stop loop with sink points ESTOP_SINK1, ESTOP_SINK2, ESTOP_SINK_LOCAL gated through SN74LVC1G07 buffers (U15, U22, U35, U36) wired as /OE-controlled sinks, feeding ESTOP_OUT shared with CAN connectors J2/J13
- Power distribution: DC-DC conversion, CM4 power-enable path (GLOBAL_EN), USB input OR-ing/protection (LTC4412 ideal-diode controller U6)
- Addressable status LEDs (WS2812B, D5-D7, D18-D21) and analog switch (ISL54222AIUZ, U5)
- RTC (PCF85063ATAAZ) referenced in notes but let me check if it's in the netlist... Actually the spec says "an RTC (datasheet link in cm4_robot_board/docs points to a PCF85063ATAAZ RTC — see new_notes.txt)". Looking at the netlist, I don't see a PCF85063 RTC component. But the spec says this is a TODO/reference link, not necessarily implemented. Let me not focus on that.

Key items from spec component table:
- U8, U9 — MCP2515-xSO CAN controllers; Y1, Y2 — 16MHz crystals. Netlist shows Y1=16MHz, Y2=16MHz. Good.
- U11 (and CAN1 counterpart) — isolated CAN transceiver; U18, U19 (SN74LVC1G07) driving TXLED/RXLED nets from U8 TXCAN/RXCAN. Let me check: netlist shows U18 and U19 are SN74LVC1G07. Net TXLED: U11.3 (TXD), U18.2 (A), U8.1 (TXCAN). Net RXLED: U11.2 (RXD), U19.2 (A), U8.2 (RXCAN). Good.
- U15, U22, U35, U36 (SN74LVC1G07) wired as /OE gates on ESTOP_SINK1/2/LOCAL. Let me check the e-stop circuit.
- U6 — LTC4412xS6 ideal-diode. Good.
- Module1 pin 99 (Global_EN) — GLOBAL_EN net, tied directly to SW1 pin 2. Netlist shows net GLOBAL_EN: Module1.99, SW1.2. Good.
- D9, D10 — CDSOT23-SM712 TVS diode arrays on CAN0_P/N, CAN1_P/N. Let me check.

Now let me look at the CAN bus connectivity carefully. This is a key area.

The spec says: "two isolated CAN buses (CAN0, CAN1), each driven by its own MCP2515 SPI CAN controller (U8, U9) through an isolated CAN transceiver (U11/companion), broken out on M12 circular connectors J2 ('CAN Interface A') and J13 ('CAN Interface B')."

So CAN0 should be: U8 (MCP2515) -> U11 (isolated transceiver) -> J2 and/or J13.
CAN1 should be: U9 (MCP2515) -> U10 (isolated transceiver) -> J2 and/or J13.

Let me look at the nets:

Net /CAN0_N: D10.1, J13.8, J2.8, R34.1, U11.6 (CANL)
Net /CAN0_P: D10.2, J13.5, J2.5, SW6.4, U11.7 (CANH)
Net /CAN1_N: D9.1, J13.3, J2.3, R35.1, U10.6 (CANL)
Net /CAN1_P: D9.2, J13.2, J2.2, SW6.3, U10.7 (CANH)

Now the CAN controller connections:
Net Net-(U10-RXD): U10.2 (RXD), U9.2 (RXCAN)
Net Net-(U10-TXD): U10.3 (TXD), U9.1 (TXCAN)
Net Net-(U11-RXD)? Let me check. Actually there's no net named U11-RXD. Let me look:
Net RXLED: U11.2 (RXD), U19.2 (A), U8.2 (RXCAN)
Net TXLED: U11.3 (TXD), U18.2 (A), U8.1 (TXCAN)

Hmm interesting. So U11's RXD (pin 2) and TXD (pin 3) are connected to U8's RXCAN (pin 2) and TXCAN (pin 1) respectively. And U10's RXD (pin 2) is connected to U9's RXCAN (pin 2), U10's TXD (pin 3) connected to U9's TXCAN (pin 1).

So:
- U8 (MCP2515 #1) <-> U11 (isolated transceiver) <-> /CAN0_P/N <-> J2, J13
- U9 (MCP2515 #2) <-> U10 (isolated transceiver) <-> /CAN1_P/N <-> J2, J13

Wait, but both CAN0 and CAN1 are broken out to BOTH J2 and J13? Let me look:
J2 (CAN Interface A) pins:
- Pin 1: ESTOP_SINK1
- Pin 2: /CAN1_P
- Pin 3: /CAN1_N
- Pin 4: GND
- Pin 5: /CAN0_P
- Pin 6: ESTOP_OUT
- Pin 7: 5V_switched_CAN
- Pin 8: /CAN0_N
- Pin 9: GND

J13 (CAN Interface B) pins:
- Pin 1: ESTOP_SINK2
- Pin 2: /CAN1_P
- Pin 3: /CAN1_N
- Pin 4: GND
- Pin 5: /CAN0_P
- Pin 6: ESTOP_OUT
- Pin 7: 5V_switched_CAN
- Pin 8: /CAN0_N
- Pin 9: GND

So both J2 and J13 carry both CAN0 and CAN1. That's a design choice (each connector exposes both buses). The spec says "broken out on M12 circular connectors J2 ('CAN Interface A') and J13 ('CAN Interface B')". This is consistent — both buses on both connectors. OK.

Now the termination resistors: R34 (120R) on /CAN0_N, R35 (120R) on /CAN1_N. The other ends:
Net Net-(R34-Pad2): R34.2, SW6.1
Net Net-(R35-Pad2): R35.2, SW6.2
SW6 is a 2-bit DIP switch. So the termination resistors are switched via SW6. That's a design choice for CAN termination enable. OK.

Now let me look at the TVS diodes D9, D10. The spec says D9, D10 — CDSOT23-SM712 TVS diode arrays on CAN0_P/N, CAN1_P/N.

CDSOT23-SM712 pinout (from libpart): pin 1 = Input, pin 2 = Input, pin 3 = Output. The SM712 is a CAN bus TVS diode array: it has two input pins (one to CANH, one to CANL) and one output pin (to GND). So pin 1 -> CANH, pin 2 -> CANL, pin 3 -> GND (or some arrangement).

Let me check D10:
Net /CAN0_N: D10.1 (Input)
Net /CAN0_P: D10.2 (Input)
Net GND: D10.3 (Output)
So D10: pin1 -> /CAN0_N, pin2 -> /CAN0_P, pin3 -> GND. Good, that's correct for a CAN TVS.

D9:
Net /CAN1_N: D9.1 (Input)
Net /CAN1_P: D9.2 (Input)
Net GND: D9.3 (Output)
Good.

Now let me look at the e-stop circuit. The spec says: "an e-stop loop with multiple sink points (ESTOP_SINK1, ESTOP_SINK2, ESTOP_SINK_LOCAL) gated through single non-inverting buffers (SN74LVC1G07, parts U15, U22, U35, U36) wired as /OE-controlled sinks, feeding an ESTOP_OUT signal shared with the CAN connectors J2/J13."

Let me trace the e-stop circuit.

SN74LVC1G07 pinout: pin 1 = /OE, pin 2 = A, pin 3 = GND, pin 4 = Y (open-drain output), pin 5 = VCC.

Net ESTOP_SINK1: J2.1, R32.1, SW7.8, U22.1 (/OE)
Net ESTOP_SINK2: J13.1, R4.1, SW7.7, U15.1 (/OE)
Net ESTOP_SINK_LOCAL: J9.1, R56.1, SW7.6, U35.1 (/OE)

So each sink point is a net that has a connector pin (where the e-stop loop wire plugs in), a pull-up resistor to +3V3 (R32, R4, R56), a DIP switch SW7 pin (for enabling/disabling that sink?), and the /OE input of a buffer.

Wait, let me check the pull-ups:
R32: pin 1 -> ESTOP_SINK1, pin 2 -> +3V3. (from netlist: R32 pin2 on +3V3, pin1 on ESTOP_SINK1). Yes.
R4: pin 1 -> ESTOP_SINK2, pin 2 -> +3V3. Yes.
R56: pin 1 -> ESTOP_SINK_LOCAL, pin 2 -> +3V3. Yes.

Now the buffers:
U22: /OE pin1 -> ESTOP_SINK1, A pin2 -> GND (from netlist: U22 pin2 on GND), Y pin4 -> Net-(U15-A), VCC pin5 -> +3V3, GND pin3 -> GND.
U15: /OE pin1 -> ESTOP_SINK2, A pin2 -> Net-(U15-A), Y pin4 -> Net-(U15-Y), VCC pin5 -> +3V3, GND pin3 -> GND.
U35: /OE pin1 -> ESTOP_SINK_LOCAL, A pin2 -> Net-(U15-Y), Y pin4 -> /ESTOP_SINK_ALL, VCC pin5 -> +3V3, GND pin3 -> GND.

Hmm wait, this is a chain of buffers. Let me re-examine. This is interesting. The SN74LVC1G07 is a non-inverting open-drain buffer with active-low output enable. When /OE is low, the output Y is enabled (can pull low); when /OE is high, Y is high-Z.

Let me look at the chain:
- U22: A = GND (tied low). /OE = ESTOP_SINK1. So when ESTOP_SINK1 is low (e-stop pressed/open?), Y pulls low. Y = Net-(U15-A).
- U15: A = Net-(U15-A). /OE = ESTOP_SINK2. Y = Net-(U15-Y).
- U35: A = Net-(U15-Y). /OE = ESTOP_SINK_LOCAL. Y = /ESTOP_SINK_ALL.
- U36: /OE = /ESTOP_SINK_ALL, A = ESTOP (GPIO6), Y = ESTOP_OUT.

Hmm, this is a chain where the outputs feed the inputs of the next. This is a weird topology. Let me think about whether this matches the spec.

Actually, the spec says these are "wired as /OE-controlled sinks". Let me look at the original reference design intent. The spec text: "an e-stop loop with multiple sink points (ESTOP_SINK1, ESTOP_SINK2, ESTOP_SINK_LOCAL) gated through single non-inverting buffers (SN74LVC1G07, parts U15, U22, U35, U36) wired as /OE-controlled sinks, feeding an ESTOP_OUT signal shared with the CAN connectors J2/J13."

Hmm. So the idea is: each sink point, when activated, sinks current to pull the ESTOP_OUT line low (or high). The buffers are open-drain, so their Y outputs are OR'd together (wired-OR) to drive ESTOP_OUT.

But in the netlist, the Y outputs are NOT all tied to ESTOP_OUT. Instead they form a chain: U22.Y -> U15.A -> ... This is strange.

Wait, let me re-examine. Let me look at the actual nets again very carefully.

Net /ESTOP_SINK_ALL: R27.2, R57.1, R63.2, U35.4 (Y), U36.1 (/OE)
Net ESTOP_OUT: D30.4 (A2), J13.6, J2.6, R60.2, U36.4 (Y)
Net ESTOP_SINK1: J2.1, R32.1, SW7.8, U22.1 (/OE)
Net ESTOP_SINK2: J13.1, R4.1, SW7.7, U15.1 (/OE)
Net ESTOP_SINK_LOCAL: J9.1, R56.1, SW7.6, U35.1 (/OE)
Net Net-(U15-A): R46.2, R61.2, U15.2 (A), U22.4 (Y)
Net Net-(U15-Y): R45.2, R62.2, U15.4 (Y), U35.2 (A)

OK so the chain is:
U22 (/OE=ESTOP_SINK1, A=GND) -> Y = Net-(U15-A)
U15 (/OE=ESTOP_SINK2, A=Net-(U15-A)) -> Y = Net-(U15-Y)
U35 (/OE=ESTOP_SINK_LOCAL, A=Net-(U15-Y)) -> Y = /ESTOP_SINK_ALL
U36 (/OE=/ESTOP_SINK_ALL, A=ESTOP[GPIO6]) -> Y = ESTOP_OUT

Hmm. This is a daisy chain of open-drain buffers. Let me think about the logic.

Actually, this is a known pattern. Let me think. Each SN74LVC1G07 has an open-drain output Y. The A input is the data input. When /OE is low (enabled), Y = A (with open drain: if A is low, Y pulls low; if A is high, Y is high-Z). When /OE is high (disabled), Y is high-Z regardless of A.

Wait, but the A inputs here: U22.A = GND (always low). U15.A = U22.Y. U35.A = U15.Y. U36.A = ESTOP (GPIO).

Hmm, this is getting complicated. Let me think about what the original design intended vs what's here.

Actually, I recall that in the real Acorn robot board, the e-stop circuit uses the buffers as sinks: each ESTOP_SINKx net, when driven low by an external e-stop button (closing the loop to ground), enables the corresponding buffer (because /OE is connected to the sink net, and the sink net is pulled up by R; when the button closes it to ground, /OE goes low, enabling the buffer). The buffer's A is tied to GND, so Y pulls the common ESTOP_OUT line low. Multiple buffers' Y outputs are tied together (wired-OR) to ESTOP_OUT.

But in THIS netlist, the buffers are chained, not OR'd. U22.Y goes to U15.A, not to ESTOP_OUT. That seems like a deviation!

Hold on. Let me look more carefully. Maybe I'm misreading the pin functions. Let me double check the SN74LVC1G07 pin mapping in the libpart:

(libpart (lib "acorn-motherboard") (part "SN74LVC1G07QDCKTQ1")
  ...
  (pins
    (pin (num "1") (name "/OE") (type "input"))
    (pin (num "2") (name "A") (type "input"))
    (pin (num "3") (name "GND") (type "power_in"))
    (pin (num "4") (name "Y") (type "output"))
    (pin (num "5") (name "VCC") (type "power_in"))))

Yes: pin1=/OE, pin2=A, pin3=GND, pin4=Y, pin5=VCC.

Now U22: pin1 (/OE) on ESTOP_SINK1, pin2 (A) on GND, pin4 (Y) on Net-(U15-A).
U15: pin1 (/OE) on ESTOP_SINK2, pin2 (A) on Net-(U15-A), pin4 (Y) on Net-(U15-Y).
U35: pin1 (/OE) on ESTOP_SINK_LOCAL, pin2 (A) on Net-(U15-Y), pin4 (Y) on /ESTOP_SINK_ALL.
U36: pin1 (/OE) on /ESTOP_SINK_ALL, pin2 (A) on ESTOP, pin4 (Y) on ESTOP_OUT.

Hmm. So this is a chain. Let me think about whether this is the intended design or an anomaly.

Actually wait. Let me reconsider. Maybe the original design DOES chain them in a particular way, OR maybe the original design has each buffer's Y tied to ESTOP_OUT (wired-OR), and the anomaly here is that the chain was rewired.

Let me look at the pull-up/pull-down resistors on the intermediate nets to understand the intended logic:

Net-(U15-A): R46.2 (130R to Net-(D29-K)? let me check), R61.2 (10k to +3V3), U15.2, U22.4.
Actually R46: pin1 on Net-(D29-K), pin2 on Net-(U15-A). R46 is 130R. Net-(D29-K): D29.1 (K), R46.1. D29 is LED_RED. D29.2 (A) on /LED_3.3V_POWER_NONINV. Hmm so D29 is an LED in series with R46 from Net-(U15-A) to /LED_3.3V_POWER_NONINV. That's a status indicator for the e-stop chain? Interesting.

Net-(U15-Y): R45.2 (130R to Net-(D28-K)), R62.2 (10k to +3V3), U15.4, U35.2.
Net-(D28-K): D28.1 (K), R45.1. D28.2 (A) on /LED_3.3V_POWER_NONINV.

/ESTOP_SINK_ALL: R27.2 (130R to Net-(D8-K)), R57.1 (2.2k to +3V3), R63.2 (10k to +3V3), U35.4, U36.1.
Net-(D8-K): D8.1 (K), R27.1. D8.2 (A) on /LED_3.3V_POWER_NONINV.

So each intermediate node has an LED (D29, D28, D8) indicating its state, plus a 10k pull-up to +3V3.

Hmm, this is a chain of open-drain buffers where each stage's output is pulled up by 10k, and the next stage's input reads that. With LEDs to indicate.

Let me think about the logic of an open-drain non-inverting buffer chain.

Stage U22: A=GND (low). /OE = ESTOP_SINK1. When ESTOP_SINK1 is LOW (enabled), Y is enabled and since A is low, Y pulls Net-(U15-A) LOW. When ESTOP_SINK1 is HIGH (disabled), Y is high-Z, and Net-(U15-A) is pulled HIGH by R61 (10k).

So Net-(U15-A) = NOT(ESTOP_SINK1_low)? Actually Net-(U15-A) is low when ESTOP_SINK1 is low (button pressed/loop closed). When ESTOP_SINK1 high (loop open), Net-(U15-A) high.

Hmm wait, but the e-stop loop: when the loop is intact (safe), what's the state of ESTOP_SINK1? The spec note says "e-stop should activate if a cable is disconnected. - nevermind, it does this". So cable disconnect (loop open) should trigger e-stop.

Let me think: ESTOP_SINK1 has a pull-up R32 (2.2k to +3V3) and connects to J2.1 (the e-stop loop wire). When the loop is closed (cable connected, e-stop not pressed), the external loop provides a path to ground? Or to +? Typically an e-stop loop is a series chain of NC contacts; when intact it's a closed circuit. The board injects current and senses. Hmm.

This is getting too deep. Let me step back and think about whether the chain topology is the anomaly or the intended design.

Actually, I found it. Let me look at the original reference. The spec describes the buffers as "wired as /OE-controlled sinks, feeding an ESTOP_OUT signal". The phrase "feeding an ESTOP_OUT signal" suggests the Y outputs feed ESTOP_OUT. In a proper sink design, all the Y outputs would be tied together to ESTOP_OUT (wired-OR), so any enabled sink pulls ESTOP_OUT low.

But here, U22.Y, U15.Y, U35.Y are NOT tied to ESTOP_OUT. Only U36.Y is tied to ESTOP_OUT. The chain is U22.Y -> U15.A, U15.Y -> U35.A, U35.Y -> U36./OE.

Hmm, but actually maybe the original design is exactly this chain, where the chain propagates the "any sink active" condition to U36's /OE, and U36's A is the GPIO ESTOP signal. Let me think.

Actually, you know, I'm not sure. Let me look at this from a different angle. Let me look at the LEDs and the intermediate pull-ups. Each intermediate node (Net-(U15-A), Net-(U15-Y), /ESTOP_SINK_ALL) has a 10k pull-up to +3V3. For an open-drain output, a pull-up is needed to define the high state. That's consistent with using Y as a signal that the next stage reads as input A. So the chain design is internally consistent: each open-drain Y is pulled up by 10k, and read by the next buffer's A.

But wait, there's also R57 (2.2k) and R63 (10k) both to +3V3 on /ESTOP_SINK_ALL. Two pull-ups? R57 = 2.2k to +3V3, R63 = 10k to +3V3. Hmm. And R27 = 130R to LED D8. So /ESTOP_SINK_ALL has two pull-ups (2.2k and 10k). That's a bit odd but not necessarily wrong.

Hmm, actually wait. Let me look at the original design's e-stop more carefully. Let me look at the actual upstream repo behavior. I recall the Acorn board e-stop uses the buffers with A tied to GND and Y tied to a common ESTOP_OUT (wired-OR), with a pull-up on ESTOP_OUT. Let me check ESTOP_OUT's pull-up: ESTOP_OUT has R60 (130R to Net-(D30-K2)), D30.4 (A2), J13.6, J2.6, U36.4. Is there a pull-up on ESTOP_OUT? R60 goes to Net-(D30-K2), which is D30.2 (K2). D30 is LED_Dual_KKAA. D30 pin4 = A2 on ESTOP_OUT, pin2 = K2 on Net-(D30-K2), R59 pin1 on Net-(D30-K1), R60 pin1 on Net-(D30-K2). R59 pin2 -> GND, R60 pin2 -> ESTOP_OUT. Hmm wait:

Net-(D30-K1): D30.1 (K1), R59.1. R59.2 -> GND.
Net-(D30-K2): D30.2 (K2), R60.1. R60.2 -> ESTOP_OUT.
D30.3 (A1) -> /LED_3.3V_POWER_NONINV.
D30.4 (A2) -> ESTOP_OUT.

So D30 is a dual LED: one LED from A1(K1 via R59 to GND) — that's a status LED driven by /LED_3.3V_POWER_NONINV. The other LED: A2 = ESTOP_OUT, K2 = Net-(D30-K2) via R60 to ESTOP_OUT?? Wait that's confusing. Let me re-read.

D30 pin4 = A2 on ESTOP_OUT. D30 pin2 = K2 on Net-(D30-K2). R60 pin1 = Net-(D30-K2), R60 pin2 = ESTOP_OUT. So the LED from A2 to K2: anode = ESTOP_OUT, cathode = Net-(D30-K2) = R60 to ESTOP_OUT. That means both ends connect to ESTOP_OUT through the LED and through R60? That would short the LED with R60 in parallel, both between ESTOP_OUT and ESTOP_OUT? No wait.

Let me carefully parse. The LED D30 internal: anode A2 (pin4) to cathode K2 (pin2). A2 is on net ESTOP_OUT. K2 is on net Net-(D30-K2). R60 connects Net-(D30-K2) (pin1) to ESTOP_OUT (pin2). So R60 is in parallel with the LED (from ESTOP_OUT through LED to Net-(D30-K2), and through R60 back to ESTOP_OUT). So the LED is shorted by R60! That can't be right for a status LED. With source=+5V, drain=VIN=0, the channel on would conduct +5V -> USB (reverse feed!). That's exactly the reverse-current scenario the protection should block, but the swapped orientation causes it to conduct.
